common_name: Tumbling Tom Yellow Tomato (Cascading Container Cherry Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Tumbling Tom Yellow is the golden-fruited counterpart to the standard red Tumbling Tom, bred for the same hanging basket and container use. Plant one per 12-inch hanging basket or 2-3 per large container.

directions: Tumbling Tom Yellow is the yellow-fruited strain sold alongside standard red Tumbling Tom, sharing the same compact, naturally trailing, pendent growth habit bred specifically for hanging baskets, window boxes, and large containers rather than staking or caging. Plants stay small, under a foot wide, but the cascading stems drape 12 to 18 inches over the basket rim, loaded with abundant small, sweet, fruity golden-yellow cherry tomatoes that ripen a few days later than the red strain. Because containers dry out faster than garden soil, water consistently and feed every 1-2 weeks with a balanced liquid fertilizer to sustain the heavy, continuous fruit set. No staking, caging, or pruning is needed; simply keep picking to encourage continued flowering, and pair it with the red strain in matched baskets for a two-tone display.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter to early spring; Index is self-fertile and can also serve as a pollinizer for other early-blooming sweet cherries planted nearby.

directions: Index is a Pacific Northwest-bred sweet cherry valued both for its own fruit and as a dependable early pollinizer for other cultivars sharing its bloom window, such as Chelan. Unlike most sweet cherries, Index is self-fertile, so a single tree will set fruit on its own, and because it flowers several days ahead of Bing it can pollinate a wide range of self-unfruitful varieties that bloom at the same early time. The fruit itself is large, glossy mahogany-red with medium-red flesh, similar in appearance to Bing but ripening several days earlier, with good firmness and rich, sweet flavor for fresh eating. Site the tree in full sun with deep, well-drained soil and choose a location with good air movement and some frost protection, since the very early bloom period carries real risk from late spring freezes. Water consistently as fruit develops to reduce cracking, and prune to an open-center form for good light penetration and airflow, which helps limit brown rot and other fungal problems in humid growing regions.
sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit Research and Extension Center
